what's the value of that when you can call it with any context? As a proof of concept, you could have it do the attack on a dummy target of your own, take the tokens up until the point where it decides you're authorised, swap out the dummy name with your desired target, and continue the session from there

Reminds me of 'NOBUS', where security agencies would believe that so long as you just don't tell anyone about a vulnerability that you discovered or introduced, nobody else would abuse that vulnerability to exploit a target while you can get access at any time. Training an LLM in such a way that it only generates the desired tokens if its memory demonstrates authorisation (surely nobody else could inject the right context otherwise) feels like a strange anthropomorphisation

children.author: nucleardog
children.textRawHtml:
"vaguely security related tasks" is right.

Found a bug in a PHP code analysis tool a while back. Not like "crash the interpreter" or anything, just the application ending up in a weird state and crashing. Couldn't exactly share our entire codebase to report the bug, so after Claude chased down _what_ the issue was, I asked it to make me a minimal reproduction so I could report the bug.

Blocked. Guessing it looked like I was trying to develop an exploit or something. By driving a static code analysis tool to an invalid state where it handled the state by cleanly reporting the issue and stopping. In an interpreted language. With the context full of Claude's own efforts to track down why and how this was happening.

Theoretically? Sure, theoretically I'm sure practically anything could be used for nefarious purposes.

Practically? Not useful in the slightest.

Funny part was--Claude was more than happy to talk with me about why it was potentially blocked and suggest ways to try and work around the guard rails. Suggested I include context like the exact bug tracker I'm reporting to, etc to try and put more weight behind the "good actor reporting a bug" aspect, etc.

I think there is a massive opportunity for this kind of feed disaggregation. Used to be the recommender and indexing of content was hard, now I believe we can likely build our own according to our own preferences.

Haiku/Sonnet (or even Jev) can do a lot of the filtering work to rank and extend an RSS feed list.

I think this gives us an opportunity to fully cut the cord from eyeball merchants who want us to maximally engage and therefore polarize their content.

children.author: ssl-3
children.textRawHtml:
Every restaurant and ghost kitchen has a reputation to uphold. They all still have customers, and those customers still chat with other people and leave reviews just like it's still 2010.

It can be easier to rebrand a ghost kitchen than to rejigger a restaurant to do other things, though. For instance: The decor doesn't even exist, much less match a certain theme.

A ghost kitchen can also do many things at once that would not traditionally fit together in a single restaurant.

I think that might be part of what some find off-putting, but there's no conceptual reason why the same location can't make awesome New Haven wood-fired pizzas, Texas smoked beef ribs, and Philly cheesesteak sandwiches on the same day. It can work as long as the volume supports each of them well-enough that they can retain workers who are able to master these things well-enough to keep a good reputation going.

It's just a building with a kitchen, and that kitchen does not have a size limit. It can do many styles of cooking at once.

And when compared to having several different sit-down restaurants to operate, management can be more-centralized while also keeping them closer to the work. This can improve quality and reduce costs.

(That doesn't make me a fan of the idea. I'd rather go to a restaurant and sit down than have anything delivered, aside from things that travel well. Pizza, BBQ, and cold subs can travel extremely well, for instance, while french fries and burgers usually turn into sadness in minutes. But other people want whatever they want and that's fine too.)
